Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations in finite systems confirm the existence of this fixed point at temperatures near the critical point. The fixed point is also found in normalized factorial cumulant behavior for at least fourth-order cumulants and is mapped into the QCD, resulting in a similar fixed point in energy dependence along different freeze-out curves in QCD.

A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares of C*-algebras, resulting in hyperfinite type II_1 subfactors of finite index and depth, is provided, utilizing Morita equivalent unitary fusion categories. We extend a prior investigation by N. Sato, generalizing his findings to encompass the broader context of such squares. Additionally, we establish a characterization for such squares yielding a given type II_1 subfactor, and this analysis contributes to a broader understanding of 4-tensors related to matrix product operators in 2-dimensional topological systems.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an optimization process with biological characteristics, reminiscent of metabolism and growth. Our experiments, spanning both artificial and real-world datasets, demonstrate that this framework outperforms comparable approaches, particularly in scenarios with optimization landscape and data dimensionality challenges.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on two widely used datasets for tasks involving human activity recognition and emotion detection, and the results show that it successfully boosts the reliability of existing models with only a modest investment of human time.

In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of professional datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a collection of high-quality xxm40000 and a innovative Lateral Inhibition Module to enhance prohibited items detection. Furthermore, to our knowledge, this is the largest and most comprehensive XXRD dataset compiled for prohibited items detection, consisting of 40,000 professional and meticulously labeled images from real-world airport security inspections. By incorporating domain-specific annotation guidelines and employing both automated and manual annotation techniques, we ensure exceptional accuracy and consistency in labeling. To further analyze prohibited items detection tasks from multiple perspectives, we design a novel Lateral Inhibition Module that emulates how human vision processes adjacent information, allowing for more effective performance enhancement. Experimental results demonstrate that our LIM outperforms existing detection methods, indicating its capability to capture contextual cues and reduce unnecessary alarms. All details regarding the compilation of xxm4000 and implementations are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengjiong1995/XXSecurityInspection.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques to enhance the WSD task.  We introduce two context-gloss augmentation techniques: (1) sentence-context augmentation and (2) synonym-augmentation, and evaluate their individual and combined effects.  Experimental results demonstrate that all proposed methods outperform the baseline, while the context-gloss double augmentation strategy yields the most favorable WSD performance.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. It also proves the connection to the traditional complex representation, in addition to obtaining a modified complex representation following the standard Hankel path.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning approaches and examines their respective vulnerabilities. We highlight the critical need for a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between formulating DP on graph data and the underlying learning algorithm and data structure. This work is conducted with the aim of highlighting key issues and potential research directions associated with graph-based differential privacy.

The vast amount of images, data, and resources that Euclid will generate positions the consortium to create comprehensive legacy databases of outstanding quality, encompassing high-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy with significant implications for the study of galaxies. These proceedings outline the promising opportunities and scientific breakthroughs Euclid will achieve in the areas of galaxy and AGN development, the evolution of the cosmos, investigations of the Milky Way, and various other celestial bodies and phenomena.

In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a stochastic Boltzmann equation that simulates non-equilibrium dynamics and found that this new framework yields more accurate results than their existing moving lattice hydrodynamic scheme when applied to systems in thermal equilibrium or when subjected to sudden changes in their container.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network, or DCAN, to generate precise action proposals. Initially, we divide the video into overlapping segments and employ multi-scale matching to create dense action boundaries. Subsequently, to aggregate long-term context, we aggregate temporal features at biologically-plausible frequencies, and a Dual-Stream Matching Network is used to evaluate the validity of action proposals. Experiments on three prominent temporal action detection benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method, surpassing the state-of-the-art performance.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently discovered connection between PTM and the edge plasma's shear Alfv\'en wave has been further explored through additional measurements at the JET facility. A unique scenario has been formulated in which a Alfv\'en wave becoming trapped within a magnetic island feedback with the edge plasma turbulence generates the PTM's characteristic shape. However, validating this concept requires very specific conditions and further experimentation is needed to ascertain its accuracy.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform.

Given an independent and identically distributed sequence of letters drawn from an alphabet $\mathcal{A}$, a sequence of words $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ is constructed by randomly selecting starting positions for $v_1$, then $v_2$, and so on, within an increasingly large number $N_n$ of letters. The principle of large deviations describes the probability of observing an empirical content $w$ in the sequence of words, and is proven to be equivalent to a variational issue involving a cost function derived from the Landau-Lifshitz equation or a direct calculation of minimal expected waiting times for patterns $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ and $w$. Notably, this calculation can be performed using existing formulas for pattern occurrence.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to the concept of meta-surfaces, which encompass the framework of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS). Lately, researchers have explored the potential of IRS to optimize target parameter estimation in radar applications. This paper builds upon this area of study by investigating a broader scenario, in which the target parameters are significantly larger than the dimensions of both the radar and IRS systems. We propose two novel approaches, Field-of-View and Image models, to model this setting and provide a unique perspective on how targets interact with both the radar and IRS systems. Field-of-View model focuses on solid angles, while the Image model projects virtual transmissions and receptions. We demonstrate the advantages of employing an IRS in radar applications by comparing the radar effective aperture in both scenarios, and propose methods for utilizing an IRS to improve target parameter estimation.

Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address (1) the enhancement of fuzzer performance in detecting sophisticated failures and (2) the development of more effective techniques for triggering mutations and faults.

Deep learning models, highly effective for certain tasks and applications, also exhibit transferable knowledge that can be applied across various fields. Build upon this, our research explores continuing to use these models beyond their initial training and fine-tuning based on newly available data. However, accessing such data over time often poses challenges due to privacy concerns and logistical constraints, resulting in a sequence of task-related information. Here, we investigate staying at par with past knowledge while learning new knowledge, resulting in the definition of continual learning. Despite significant progress, current frameworks typically exhibit improvement, resulting in significant drops, when models based on pretrained models are compared to those from scratch. Here, we challenge this assumption and demonstrate that such models perform similarly to those from scratch. Here, we derive theoretical justification for this finding, raising questions about the utility of pretrained models in continual learning settings.

We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solutions $u$ to the given semilinear parabolic equation on the real line. These bounded solutions $u$ of the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + f(u)$, where the initial data have distinct finite limits, were examined earlier with specific conditions on the function $f$ being locally Lipschitz on the real line. This time we explore a scenario in which the function $f$ satisfies particular equilibrium conditions, specifically where $\theta^\pm = \overline{u}$ and $f(\theta^\pm) = 0$. This report delves into the scenario in which the limits $\theta^+$ and $\theta^-$ are unrelated to one another. Having already presented descriptions of convergent solutions involving stable limits at infinity in two prior publications, we now have a thorough understanding of solution behaviors in this final situation.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes.

Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a category of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games where each player's payoff function is influenced by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz rate in response to other players' actions. Their work demonstrated that these types of games have the capacity for achieving $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$ conditions. Despite their findings, they left unspecified the $\epsilon$ parameter's minimum value able to satisfy the requirements for such an equilibrium. In this research, we make advancements on various fronts, including obtaining higher bounds for query complexity, establishing lower bounds for the query complexity of determining $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $\Omega(\sqrt{k}\lambda/(\epsilon^{2.5}\log(1/\epsilon)))$; establishing lower bounds for sample complexity as well as information complexity in relation to finding $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in Lipschitz games, and finally, showing that our query complexity lower bound holds even within the context of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games involving two players. These information complexity lower bounds are relevant regardless of whether we are discussing approximate pure Nash equilibria in Lipschitz games or exact pure Nash equilibria in games with higher complexity. Given that our query complexity lower bound corresponds to five previous bounds but with significantly tighter values, it approaches indication that $\epsilon$ parameters unable to satisfy the requirements for

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K and a larger J when tuning parameters, and we validate our approach across diverse NLP tasks such as part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and semi-supervised task tuning.

Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research has successfully integrated Teacher-Student architectures with advanced pretraining techniques like BERT and GPT, leading to notable enhancements in the effectiveness of these models. This paper explores the diverse applications of Teacher-Student architectures, analyzes their key pretraining methods, and summarizes their knowledge-learning capabilities. Moreover, it highlights existing challenges and potential research directions. By doing so, this work aims to provide a clear understanding of Teacher-Student architectures and their broad implications on the field of knowledge learning.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, offering an innovative perspective on its structure. Additionally, the series known as the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be computed explicitly. The research discussed also extends towards the special Askey-Wilson algebra as well as more complex, higher rank variants of the same, allowing further exploration of its underlying principles.

Our study shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon
excitations may offer a suitable path to achieving magnetic analogs of twisted
superfluid and supersolid phases previously found in ultracold atomic condensates
trapped in optical lattices. Employing a cluster Gutzwiller mean-field theory,
we prove that Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions are responsible for stabilizing
these phases within a magnetic framework, in contrast to the technical requirements
of twisted wavefunctions and intermixing of species needed in atomic systems.
Furthermore, we indicate that the twisted superfluid phase can be associated
with a D3 quantum disordered state, while the twisted supersolid phase may be
described as having a liquid crystal order in its spin component.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information.

We are suggesting the establishment of a state-of-the-art muon-proton and muon-nucleus collider that operates at the TeV level, capable of delivering high-statistical data for both QCD studies and physics beyond the Standard Model. We have considered various processes and discovered that precise measurements of scattering processes could be made with minimal uncertainty from the beam, particularly when it comes to differential cross-sections. If necessary, even the structure of particles at a sub-atomic level could be studied, with forward scattering measurements providing a robust check for other methods. Should new anomalies appear in QCD data, they could be thoroughly investigated with di-lepton production as a clean process. We have also highlighted the potential for adding an electron beam to create muon-electron collision capabilities.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial for generating high-quality images rapidly. To test this method, the procedure involved creating the sequence and running it on four healthy volunteers. Traditional slice-to-stack ordering was compared to a proposed reverse-randome-raid (R3) ordering. Additionally, different readout readout durations (44 and 110ms) were tested. Two approaches were used to assess image quality: a global approach, which ranks the best and worst images, and a more comprehensive approach, which maps out all possible outcomes. It was found that the R3 ordering provided significantly better results than the WS ordering (p<0.05). Moreover, the approach allowed for selecting readout durations that balanced spatial resolution and coverage (p<0.05). Most importantly, the procedure yielded excellent image quality in a consistent anatomical area (p<0.05). These results indicate that the study's findings support the use of the R3 readout ordering, the selected readout duration, and the comprehensive approach to improve image quality.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous.

In this work, domains are represented by equipping suitable families with an order based on set inclusion from specific mathematical structures. The focus here is on domain representations via approximation spaces with CF-structures, which involve introducing the concepts of CF-approximation spaces and CF-closed sets. It is demonstrated that the collection of CF-closed sets in a CF-approximation space, ordered by inclusion, forms a continuous domain and every continuous domain can be mapped isomorphically to a collection of CF-closed sets in a CF-approximation space. Building on this foundation, the notion of relations approximable by CF is developed using a categorical perspective, which enables the preservation of certain mathematical properties of relations under cofinite limit operations in a category.

The paired-permutation test, a popular method in neuroscience for identifying coherent neural activity patterns, has been utilized to detect coordinated neural firing that distinguishes between two scenarios. This testing method evaluates the paired correlation matrix between the scenarios and compares it to an null distribution generated by creating random combinations of the data sets. Due to the large size of necessary sample sizes for exact calculations, a common practice involves using random sampling methods. However, this introduces inaccuracies in p-value estimates. We investigate the parameters that influence permutation approximation errors and establish the minimum required samples for achieving desired accuracy.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior.

We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space.

Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of the graph connections. To address this issue, we propose a strategy to simplify the graph structure by selectively removing unnecessary edges, keeping the node features intact. This approach is designed to maintain high performance while making the graph more easy to understand, particularly when worked in collaboration with node-focused visualization tools. By leveraging pre-trained node-based neural networks and leveraging existing graph structures, our method efficiently learns to sparsify the graph structure. The result is a more interpreducible model that delivers comparable performance to the original model.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by input histories, rendering it unreliable. In contrast, under randomization assumptions, we have developed an enhanced estimator that significantly boosts the recall and precision scores by just a factor of O(log^2(1/δ)) compared to the traditional method, based on any prior input history.

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature can be conformally deformed to reveal related minimal geometries sharing key characteristics. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries.

A liquid consisting of superconducting vortices experiences an unusual response when subjected to a temperature and magnetic field that induces a thermal gradient. This reaction is characterized by a sudden increase in the transverse electric field that peaks at a specific point and then drops. This peak amplitude remains consistent across various types of superconductors despite their differences, which poses an interesting phenomenon to investigate further. This peak is essentially a representation of the minimum viscosity-to-entropy density ratio, which occurs when the entropy carried by the vortex lines is limited. This limitation is L-rope like in nature, which means that the vortex lines carry a fixed amount of entropy for a given overlap length. As the viscosity-to-entropy density ratio rises above this minimum value, the neutral vortex lines start to collide and repel in a temperature and viscosity-dependent manner. This collision and repulsion is also evident in the behavior of the Nernst response.

Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Key properties of MEF include ensuring optimal operation, providing sufficient information for accurate predictions, and enabling the development of a simple linear predictive controller. Furthermore, this approach can be applied to other processable flexibility aggregators, with numerical results showcasing the efficiency and robustness of the proposed method under various prediction scenarios.

The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning's ability to accurately predict time series data has been consistently demonstrated. In the realm of technical analysis, using indicators is the most widely adopted approach among traders and investors. Another essential aspect is sentiment analysis, which reflects the emotional state of market investors. Emotions often influence market prices and are typically amplified due to herding effects, leading to the development of a novel framework that incorporates hidden variables and market sentiment. This proposed model utilizes Generative Adversarial Networks to project stock prices and employs a BERT-based approach analysis to assess the emotional state of investors. It was tested on the DAX 30 index and outperformed the conventional methods of Neural Network and ARIMA models.

One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are exacerbated by our lack of understanding of the CE phase. This is particularly true for CE scenarios that involve stars still on their main sequence, which are often difficult to observe. This difficulty is compounded by potential inaccuracies in current models, which often rely on the assumption that the stars are in spherical shapes, an assumption that is invalid during scenarios like the spiral-in process, which involves stars deforming and experiencing complex hydrodynamic interactions, particularly when they closely approach each other and potentially collide, and which can significantly impact the binary's merger dynamics. This research aims to employ state-of-the-art simulations, utilizing the SAMRAI adaptive mesh refinement code to simulate a specific CE scenario, where both components of a binary system, with masses of 1.25 and 1.0

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess in detail, including all relevant polarizations of the W-bosons. This detailed calculation allows for a precise expression of the effective triple-Higgs coupling in terms of dimension-6 and dimension-8 operators within the two EFTs. We then estimate the impact of a potential four-boson contact interaction in the dimension-8 sector of HEFT. To assess the potential of these machines for studying Higgs physics, we analyze the sensitivity to BSM Higgs properties in double Higgs events at CLIC and ILC, particularly in scenarios where the four-W-boson interaction strength is either strong or weak, and we provide estimates for the S-matrix unitarity bounds in the two EFTs.

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization, thereby facilitating an
analytical $1/c^2$ expansion of general relativity. Ultimately, this method
permits an in-depth examination of the Einstein-Hilbert action expansion up to
its next-to-next-to-leading order.

A new computational framework is introduced to speed up the calculation of localized shocks in a five-dimensional space that mimics anti-gravity, by simplifying the complex Einstein equations. It's discovered that using a first-order approximation yields highly accurate results, which can be broken down into two manageable sets of equations. Further, it's observed that one set has minimal impact on boundary measurements, allowing the calculation to be streamlined. This improvement results in significantly faster numerical solutions, with minimal errors, at roughly one-tenth the original time for specific conditions.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and glass spheres, as it moved perpendicular to its length. We analyzed the drag in both directions and found the difference between them, a phenomenon known as anisotropy. We found that the anisotropy could be described by the ratio of the cylinder's length to the diameter of the fluidized bed. We believe this study is among the first of its kind, examining drag anisotropy in a bed of granular material.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces, small tuning datasets, and the difficulty of designing effective prior distributions. We present BoGraph, a novel structured Bayesian optimization method from logs that utilizes an acyclic graph to represent prior distributions. We analyze a decoupled optimization problem, where the nodes of the graph are independent probabilistic regreSSions. We demonstrate our approach's efficiency and effectiveness by applying it to configure BLIS and MKL-D3, achieving significant performance improvements of up to 1.5x and 1.3x respectively. An open-source implementation of BoGraph is also available.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.

When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models.

This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec from three high-axis-ratio Seyfert galaxies. The findings reveal significant chemical variations, with some regions showing up to two-fold differences between neighbors. Notably, chemical patterns align with nuclear structure geometry, with a distinct feature discovered in all samples: emission outside the Seyfert's ionization axis exhibits an "outside-in" structure, contrasting with the typical "inside-out" pattern. This new emission also shows a temperature gradient, increasing as a power law, mirroring previous findings. Furthermore, we observe a correlation between electron density and metallicity in regions longer than 0.1 kiloparsec, with an exception noted for a specific region (G3-1.6-0.6) where high metallicity coexists with low density. This exception highlights the importance of considering spatial dimension when studying chemical patterns, paving the way for a deeper understanding of galaxy interactions and interactions with dust.

As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation in the system, as well as in suppressed charm quark transitions, by initially analyzing a significant dataset from the LHC containing 2010 data. Furthermore, the ATLAS experiment has continued to investigate the beauty meson phenomena, including CPT symmetry in the neutral B meson system, the rare decay of D^0 mesons into pairs of muons, and precise determinations of flavor-specific and CP-conserving charm quark transitions, based on an analysis of a significantly enhanced dataset at centre-of-mass energies of 7 TeV and 8 TeV.

The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently, some methods have been successfully applied to simpler elements of a scene, such as road surfaces, but tackling the complex interactions between vehicles presents a greater challenge.
To address this issue, we introduce SceneGen, a stochastic model that learns to generate realistic traffic scenes based on a given road map, including the implicit interactions between vehicles.
This model is composed of two components: a base generator that produces individual vehicles and a refinement network that modifies the output of the generator by applying traffic rules and simplifying the scene.
Our experiments on real-world data demonstrate that the trained model can accurately predict traffic patterns and produce more plausible traffic scenes compared to the results of the base generator alone.
We also conduct additional experiments on synthetic data from CARLC v2.0, and the outcomes are utilized to evaluate the performance of various scene completion techniques, including our proposed two-stage approach which achieves the most accurate predictions.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems.

A group of integer sequences can be classified as jointly ergodic if for every ergodic system with a measure-preserving nature, their average values, determined by iteratively applying the sequences, converge on average to a specific, integrated product that aligns with the original values. We have derived flexible criteria that can not only verify ergodicity across most known sequence combinations, but also enable resolution for some outstanding issues. Notably, our reasoning employs a novel ergodic variant of a technique initially explored by Peluse and Prendiville in establishing quantitative versions of the finitary Szemer\'edi theorem's application.

We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located within low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) molecular clouds.
Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect superbubble dynamics and dust grain formation. Our goals were to
understand dust grain growth within clumps orbiting the superbubble, as well as
dust survival from supernovae in a highly distorted and expanding supershell.
The model accounted for cluster self-gravity and star cluster potential, while
considering cooling effects and dust influences, using a sophisticated cluster
synthesis model. Similar to previous research, clumpy media cause superbubbles
to become irregularly shaped and driven mostly by expanding hot gas through low
density pathways. Our findings suggest that in large ($\sim 10^7M_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds hosting large ($\sim 5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot}$) superclusters, dust grain growth
within clumps contributes to dust formation within $1$ Myr. However, pair-instability
and core-collapse supernovae expand the supershell rapidly, reducing internal
density and halting dust growth. Despite this, dust grain growth reaches $\sim 10^{-5}\mu
m$ in $\sim 1$

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize far-field detection because a significant number of objects in them are located close to the sensor, or in the so-called near-field. As a result, current methods struggle when it comes to detecting objects in these remote distances. We introduce Far3Det, a framework dedicated to improving three-dimensional far-field detection. It involves filtering out objects in the near-field, augmenting data by moving objects in new locations, and correcting inaccuracies introduced during this process. We also propose utilizing lidar intensity and RGB images to train networks that specialize in far-field detection. Our approach is evaluated in the NuScenes environment and demonstrates notable improvements, including detecting nearly 30% more objects with three or more levels of confidence using just lidar data.

Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES), which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, as the number of particles increases, this tool becomes impractical for applications in quantum chemistry due to challenges in measuring and generating data required for subsequent machine learning training. Our research overcomes this limitation by developing a quantum machine learning algorithm capable of learning PES from direct observations of molecular behavior. Leveraging the parameters of a parameterized quantum circuit, this model can evaluate the system's wave function at any given configuration of molecular nuclei, leading to a direct estimation of the potential energy surface. Initial tests conducted on small diatomic and triatomic molecules in the presence of external magnetic fields have validated the effectiveness of this approach, even when trained on limited datasets consisting only of ground state measurements.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset consists of synthetic surface realizations, generated using a biomechanical simulation that incorporates patient-specific material properties and forces, as well as surface features. This allows for a efficient, implicit description of the organ model, enabling a trained network to rapidly identify surface correspondences and non-rigidly register with the intraoperative video footage. The results of our experiments, conducted with simulated and real data, show that the proposed method achieves highly accurate and dense volume-to-surface registrations in under a second, making it suitable for real-time application.

For a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, research has focused on conformal matter collineations within the energy-momentum tensor. The overall structure of these collineations is determined under non-degenerate conditions, with fifteen distinct, independent forms found. However, when the energy-momentum tensor becomes degenerate, the associated conformal collineations exhibit infinite degrees of freedom. Moreover, specific degenerate subcases may still harbor non-degenerate Ricci inheritance collineations.

Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is costly and computationally intensive. Moreover, training data often lacks activity labels and robust flow predictions are not always accurate. To address these obstacles, we explore the potential of training models using unlabeled video input and pre-trained predictors, although this approach results in models learning incorrect data due to compounded errors. Consequently, we developed a self-supervised method to train adversarial metric embeddings of flow estimates, allowing a compressed neural network to predict plausible flow estimates from model outputs. To enhance training efficiency, we implemented a composite loss function that balances accuracy and confusion among clusters. We tested this approach on the KITTI Flow dataset and discovered that our method produces high-quality predictions with significantly reduced reliance on labeled data. Additionally, the proposed method yields high-quality predictions with only 5% labeled data.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing, a cutting-edge computing approach that mimics how real brains process and interpret information, offers the potential to overcome these obstacles by delivering faster, more efficient neural network performance. This has sparked considerable interest in developing specialized spiking artificial neural network processors. Despite many attempts to create these processors, there is still a pressing need for advancements in algorithms that can optimize their classification accuracy and efficiency. This research proposal aims to address this gap by introducing a novel algorithm, specifically a Random Neural Network (RNN) tailored to operate in conjunction with spiking artificial neural network processors using the LSMoE activation function.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), as demonstrated in our paper. We have generalised a previous result by Volkmann from 2007, by showing that cubic planar bipartite graphs with specific cycle lengths will be E2F, provided they do not contain certain subgraphs. Additionally, we have obtained similar proof for non-planar bipartite cubic graphs with uniform cycle lengths.

Recent research on block designs by Amarra, Devillers, and Praeger, involving specific quadratic polynomials, shows potential connections to two influential conjectures. The Bunyakovsky Conjecture would yield a crucial implication - infinitely many instances of the required designs. A vast number of prime values of the involved polynomials have been found and their quantities match closely the expectations based on a refined variant of the Bateman-Horn Conjecture. Although the infinite prime values of the polynomials have yet to be definitively confirmed, the results provide significant support for both the Bunyakovsky and Bateman-Horn Conjectures.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system.

Investigating global $B-L$ symmetry within the Standard Model is necessary due to the anomaly cancellation requirements which necessitate three right-handed neutrinos that enable the natural generation of small Standard Model neutrino masses through the seesaw mechanism. Within an extension of the Standard Model featuring a $B-L$ symmetry, we introduce a pseudo-Goldstone boson dark matter framework where the imaginary component of a complex $B-L$ Higgs field constitutes the dark matter present in the universe. The universe's dark matter abundance is dictated by the Standard Model Higgs boson-mediated process, yet its interaction with nucleons via the exchange of Higgs bosons is heavily suppressed due to its pseudo-Goldstone nature. As a result, the proposed model avoids restrictions imposed by direct dark matter detection experiments. Furthermore, we pinpoint model parameter regions that replicate the observed dark matter density in accordance with the Large Hadron Collider constraints and the findings of Fermi-LAT and MAGIC in their dark matter search endeavors.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where the birth model is represented as a set of discrete locations within a defined space. The discrete location-based model, although widely utilized in target tracking, comes with challenges due to parameter explosion when the defined space is large. A novel approach is proposed utilizing a partially grid-based birth model, which reduces the degree of freedom of target tracking while maintaining the efficiency of the prediction step. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated through a case study involving the selection of active sensors for tracking space debris.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making.

High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging.  While these methods provide initial solutions quickly, their convergence rates are insufficient for high-quality results. Formulations of ESI exist in both frequency and time domains, with the latter requiring significantly less computational resources but untested at large-scale. This research introduces an time-domain ESI formulation, develops two efficient wavefield reconstruction methods, and produces high-quality, detailed seismic images within a reasonable timeframe.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We observed isolation ratios greater than 40 dB in optical diodes, as well as a high fidelity rate for quasi-circulators. We also found that our method allows for nonreciprocal amplification of weak optical signals.

We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics.

Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

The surge in remotely accessible activities has necessitated developing systems that can be accessed from a distance. To this end, we have developed a system that allows a user to obtain two-dimensional results from a 2D LDV on a test panel from a remote location. The user can control the LDV from a computer that is not the one on which the system resides, resulting in a more efficient and cost-effective approach to achieving this. The system we propose utilizes a 2D LDV system, an interface, and the open-source software platform, TensorFlow Lite, to scan a single point in space at a rate of 40 Hz and obtain a 250 kilohertz sample rate, ultimately delivering 2-dimensional measurements with 98.65% accuracy with 250,000 measurements.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate these models based on their overall performance in generating the desired dialogue, there's a lack of clarity regarding which aspects of the encoded representation actually contribute to this encoding process. Our study investigates the internal working of three prominent generative dialogue models to analyze their low-dimensional space and understand which features of user input are actually encoded. Our findings reveal significant variations in encoding behavior across these models and suggest a distinction between "task-informed" and "task-irrelevant" components of user input. Furthermore, our research highlights the potential for improving model performance by selectively manipulating these components, which could provide valuable insights for the development of more transparent and efficient machine learning models.

Deep learning methods have gained popularity in image-based 2D place recognition but this approach has limitations when applied to LiDAR data, which lacks color and has lower resolution. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel, multi-layered deep learning framework called AttDLNet that incorporates spherical spatial binning, an IRNet encoder, and an attention mechanism to handle LiDAR data for 2D place recognition. Experimental results show that our network outperforms other spherical spatial encoding methods and can achieve robust, embedding-driven 50-way classification accuracy of 58.1% on the nuScenes dataset.

Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-On-Demand or live, demands transcoding to accommodate viewer devices. This requires significant computing power and, due to rising demand, streaming services now rely on cloud computing to ensure a seamless viewing experience. Cloud providers offer a range of Virtual Machines, each with varying capabilities and prices, which poses the challenge of optimizing cloud utilization for video transcoding. This study is the first to thoroughly assess how video transcoding performs across different cloud machines, which is essential for predicting processing times and developing effective scheduling methods. Based on this analysis and the cost variability of cloud machines, the research provides a model that helps evaluate the suitability of each cloud machine for different transcoding tasks. This model can provide resource provisioning with the best balance of performance and cost, thus enhancing the efficient use of cloud services for video streaming.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

Q-ball studies in a single symmetry theory are common, yet the field can be more expansive, allowing for the examination of theories featuring multiple symmetries in a more general context.
