This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, we can utilize data from the muonium decay rate and LSND production and decay patterns to evaluate this scalar's coupling, excluding the mass window indicated by the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly in the electron-muon sector. Furthermore, we analyze three major production processes of these scalar particles at beam dump experiments, such as the Drell-Yan process, heavy meson decay, and muon scattering, to derive constraints from the CHARM II detection of muon neutrinos produced at CERN in 1987. Consequently, we summarize and visualize the exclusion and permitted regions of this theoretical model's parameter space, utilizing the data from these experiments.

This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in an engineering program. Focusing on students in the second and third years of the program, data was collected through online surveys in April 2020, after two weeks of remote instruction had been implemented. The research sample comprised 301 students and data was analyzed using Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings revealed significant variations among different student groups, with those accustomed to remote learning and with high self-discipline showing greater ability to stay on track. Conversely, students lacking access to necessary technology and with lower English proficiency struggled more. These results highlight the heterogeneous nature of remote learning's impact, emphasizing the need for tailored support strategies to address the diverse challenges faced by students during the pandemic.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent, yet in Liouville conformal field theory, it becomes obscure. Using correlation functions and spectral representations, we offer a set of analytic continuations for Fourier-Legendre transforms of correlation functions. This is achieved through contour integrals, which are then used to derive explicit formulas for spin conservation laws. These expressions for the Fourier transforms of correlation functions, combined with the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Ward identities, are applied to obtain precise values for the three-point coefficient $C_{ppp}(p_1,p_2,p_3)$, a previously unresolved problem.
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, if this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass and charge configuration.

In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly, axiomatic paracomplete and paraconsistent
version of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, incorporating a user-defined pairing
axiom. Our analysis reveals that this updated framework is equivalent to its
classical Zermelo-Fraenkel counterpart.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting step rates during single-cue conditions and a novel decision framework was developed to achieve 93.6% accuracy in detecting step onsets in mixed-trial conditions. Furthermore, an exploration of walking states was facilitated by incorporating angular velocity and step rate features, yielding 3 distinctly classified states with 98.8% average accuracy. These findings highlight the potential for high-resolution spatial and temporal resolution imaging techniques to facilitate the design of advanced BCI-driven therapies for gait rehabilitation.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, their application to dynamic systems remains limited. This study proposes a novel graph-based neural network model, named Dynamic Effective Connectivity (DEC), that can estimate dynamic connectivity patterns, particularly those resembling human brain activity. DEC combines an initial graph learning phase with a time-varying state space model to first identify the structure of a system and then refine its dynamic characteristics. By utilizing likelihood functions and variational inference, we can infer both aspects of DEC. Experiments show that DEC outperforms relevant classification and prediction benchmarks and demonstrate its flexibility in employing alternative graph learning models.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators, and reproducing. The field of ethology, or the scientific study of animal behavior, relies on observing and analyzing animal behavior to gain insights. However, manually collecting and analyzing data from video footage of moving creatures can be time-consuming and subjective. We developed a computational method to extract information about animal locomotion from video, which includes identifying and labeling a single biological creature as it moves through the frame. When tested on multiple datasets, our method correctly detected and tracked 93.3% of biological locomotion, outperforming existing methods such as the traditional way of analyzing motion (33.3% recall) and using optical flow, which achieved a comparable result of 89.6% recall.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic iterative methods, including techniques like Kramers-Kronig (KK) and their generalizations (GKK). This paper introduces a novel approach, K'K, which extends the GKK family and can be customized to prioritize either speed or precision. When K'K is set to KK, it outperforms other methods such as GKK, SOR, and BSOR, particularly for dense matrices. Furthermore, the K'K method's graph-state interpretation has led to the creation of a new algorithm, Q'Q, which shows superior performance in sparse matrices.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the macroscopically disordered momentum-space model. Additionally, we extend this analysis to include quadrupole disordered cases, finding that correlated disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in a new parameter range.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies.

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion at the N^3LL' level for the on-shell Higgs cross-section. The NLO QCD corrections to the bottom-quark contribution are derived within the effective field theory framework, considering both scalar bottom-quark and gluino-quark-sbottom interactions. The analysis also considers the NLO SUSY QCD corrections to the on-shell Higgs cross-section, with an estimate of the NLO SUSY QCD correction to the bottom-quark contribution. The on-shell Higgs cross-section is calculated within the MSSM with complex parameters, with a focus on the impact of supersymmetric corrections and the dependence on the MSSM parameter space. The analysis employs the full on-shell Higgs production code, with a emphasis on the impact of SUSY QCD corrections and the derivation of effective couplings for the light CP-even Higgs boson.

A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. A simulation study and empirical analysis provide further insight into the test's performance.

Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of combining differentiable optimizers with neural networks by differentiating through the solution of optimization problems. Building on this, our study aims to enhance such models by incorporating prior knowledge about the structure of the underlying problems. Specifically, we focus on applications that involve semidefinite programs and explore two areas where problems exhibit significant sparsity: reducing the variables in the Hamiltonian commutative optimization problem and the indices of support vector machines. To test our proposed methods, we apply them to real-world datasets for classification and a synthetic dataset for phase estimation. Our results demonstrate the necessity of leveraging problem structure to achieve model improvements.

A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells should be viewed as dynamic systems with reorganizing components, where boundary forces, signaling inputs, and feedback processes must be taken into account. In this paper, we propose a framework for modeling cellular spreading and motility, accounting for these factors on advecting lipid membranes. To illustrate this framework, we incorporate an external stimulus model based on cell adhesion and develop a method for relocating membrane proteins through a combination of adhesion, motility, and other cell motility mechanisms.

The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in user transactions on the Ethereum blockchain, in an effort to identify anomalies indicative of malicious activities. To operationalize this research, we develop two cyclic-anomaly detection models based on isolation forests. Furthermore, we apply our methods to a real-world dataset from the Ethereum blockchain to demonstrate their effectiveness, in terms of detection accuracy and efficiency. Our findings suggest that our approach performs exceptionally well, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.955 with only 0.015 seconds spent on analysis per transaction address.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving classical decoder agents interacting with a environment, utilizing a reinforcement learning approach to find effective decoding strategies. We develop multiple simplified models that capture the interaction between code, error, and decoder, then apply reinforcement learning to discover effective surface code decoding policies, even when accounting for measurement errors. These discovered policies demonstrate superior performance compared to previously published decoding algorithms, including the HTTP protocol, in tests simulating the continuous superposition of states.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of a global parameter within an isolated system consisting of two interconnected cavities, each containing identical atomic ensembles. By employing binary quantum feedback based on the observed jump information, we are able to achieve the same level of precision as with a highly entangled state, but using a more practical local quantum state.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that hadrons with low transverse momentum in Au$+$Au collisions have suppressed yields compared to $d$$+$Au collisions, which in turn are suppressed relative to $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Conversely, hadrons with high transverse momentum show enhanced production in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions relative to $p$$+$$p$ collisions. These findings provide quantitative evidence for initial state and final state interactions.

This paper explores the behavior of Smarandache's sequence from the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS) at A061076, specifically focusing on its associated sequences, A061077 and A061078, linked to the Smarandache's sigma product of digits. We address open questions by identifying upper bounds applicable to all natural numbers 'n', as well as deriving closed formulas for sequences 'a(n)' and 'b(n)'. Our combined results provide insights into the behavior of the broader Smarandache's sigma product sequence 'c(n)'.

Cloud-based HPC deployments can provide cost savings and optimal resource allocation.
However, there are significant differences between the network architectures of cloud and on-premise HPC systems.
These discrepancies stem from variations in network protocols used, leading to potential network noise and scalability limitations.
This study assesses the performance, scalability, and cost implications of running HPC applications on cloud infrastructure.
Initially, the investigation focuses on latency, bandwidth, and data transfer patterns in small-scale tests, followed by simulations on a large-scale cluster.
The results reveal that certain algorithms may be suitable for cloud deployment, while others require careful selection or optimization to avoid performance bottlenecks and unnecessary costs.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and a new approach is presented. This approach uses approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the context distribution is unknown and uses zero bits when the distribution is known. This approach offers nearly the same regret bound as if contexts were fully observable. This achievement is notable as it outperforms existing bounds by a significant margin. This achievement particularly occurred when the time horizon is substantial. When the distribution is known the approach offers an information theoretically optimal bound.

Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies, particularly Scrum, to maintain productivity. However, the transition to remote working has also brought about several challenges that could hinder the effectiveness of Scrum. Our research focuses on understanding how remote working influences the success of Scrum projects and the key factors that facilitate their achievement. In order to gain both theoretical and empirical insights, we combined survey data with in-depth interviews to explore how teams navigate their projects remotely. Our findings highlight the importance of face-to-face meetings, open communication channels, and the use of collaboration tools in promoting face-to-face visibility. Additionally, we emphasize the need for clear processes, defined roles, and the utilization of collaboration tools to manage face-to-face overload. By integrating our results, we can enhance our understanding of how Scrum projects can be successfully executed in a remote working environment and contribute to the broader debate surrounding remote working practices.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances causal inference using machine learning through optimal individualized treatment rules. Building on DTRs' resilience to distributional errors, our research expands previous findings. To improve readability for a broader audience, we have simplified the mathematical notation, with substantive content remaining largely consistent, though a technical assumption is clarified. Our initial study was driven by the limitation of existing DTRs' sample efficiency, which hinders optimal learning with bounded norms. We propose a novel, optimal with beta-norms, distributionally robust POITR learning algorithm, along with a new fundamental threshold for this scenario. Additionally, we are exploring an application of our robust method in the context of choice learning with bounded norms.

Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.

This paper proposes the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform as a derivative of the Linear Canonical Transform, and proves related inequalities, including Heisenberg's Inequality and a logarithmic inequality for LCST.

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large-scale $K$ user interference networks, which is known to expand without bound as the network size increases. Contrary to previous research, which primarily concentrated on topological reconfiguration, our study shifts the focus to the benefits of optimal power control. We utilize lower and upper GDoF bounds to demonstrate that, in contrast to binary on/off power control, a substantial group of powerset codes provides an extremal GDoF gain that grows at a rate of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

A significant issue with legged locomotion research is the un predictable nature of real-world terrain interaction. To address this challenge, creating mathematical models of terrain that can be used for simulation and optimization purposes has become a significant area of focus. Previously developed by the author, a novel damping-based terrain model was introduced, which accurately captures the dynamic behavior of soft terrain interactions and has since been applied in various studies involving simulation, gait optimization, and control. To fully utilize this terrain model, a corresponding method for integrating it into the equations of motion for multi-rigid body systems was also developed, allowing the model to be utilized for legged robot dynamics, motion planning, and control. This research framework led to the creation of a two-legged hopping robot, called DoublePileBot, and its controls were successfully tested in practice, with the model's accuracy validated through comparing single-pilebot behavior on simulated and real-world terrain. The results demonstrated that the developing board's damping properties were accurately modeled, with implications for future designs of legged locomotion systems.

In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values.

Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass.

Effective communication through language relies on both understanding explicit statements and implicit expectations. While anticipating open information can be achieved by analyzing linguistic cues, predicting information that is not stated can require negation reasoning. We can examine negation in two contexts: contradictory negation, which occurs when a statement directly contradicts another, and confounding negation, which arises when a statement is not supported by another. To test a model's ability to handle negation in a real-world setting, we created CONDAQA, a new dataset that is substantially larger than previously existing ones. This comprises 12,384 questions, spanning eight different domains, that require a language model to interpret contradictory and confounding negation, go beyond explicit information, and consider background knowledge. Notably, we found that current state-of-the-art open-question answering models struggle to handle CONDAQA, particularly questions that involve confounding negation. Furthermore, analysis indicates that successful answers to questions with negation can be reached by generating and ranking multiple possible answers, thereby allowing the model to choose the best option.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications, and its success heavily relies on a slow enough annealing schedule that quench dynamics are synonymous with backward quenching. Conversely, quantum quenching arises from sudden parameter shifts within a quasiclosed system, and researchers study highly initial-state-specific quantum trajectories and their typical quench growth rates, particularly within complex, combinatorial optimization problems, where both annealing and quenching procedures can provide valuable insights into the system's phases. Through investigation of the random 3SAT problem, we simulate quantum annealing protocols and analyze the resulting trajectories, noting a distinct phase transition in the order parameter's exponential growth rate, which serves as an indicator of the annealing gap and is also observable in backward quenching, and we discuss the implications of this connection on quantum annealing performance.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data.

Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite-layer nickelate, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model by
assessing various correlation effects. Notably, we find that screening plays a
significant role in shaping the material's properties. Additionally, we
determine the level of screening required to effectively reduce the two-band
model to its one-band counterpart. Furthermore, we examine how this reduction
behaves under different levels of external pressure and supercharging.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes rather than decaying properties, it reveals that the solution's deviation from the equilibrium grows at a rate of $t^\frac{5s-4}{s+3}$, in line with the proposed Taylor dispersion phenomenon for generic initial conditions.

We use radiance data from space to study wave slopes in oceans during the day, specifically using about 200 channels between 3.6 and 4.0 $\mu$m to calculate a sun glint mask that ensures a calm sea. By comparing the observed and calculated radiances, we derive wave slope statistics for a variety of sea areas. Our results are consistent with previous findings, but our study is more extensive, covering a larger range of sea conditions. We compare our cross-wave spectrum calculations to the Cox-Munk model, noting discrepancies at higher wavenumbers that may be due to a non-Gaussian distribution of deep-sea waves, as suggested by numerical models and direct measurements.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
to ensure system stability. However, pinpointing system parts that require
re-testing after a modification is a complex task. This paper presents a novel
approach to efficient test case selection for regression testing, leveraging
singular value decomposition. A specific algorithm is designed to identify
highly interconnected system modules through pairwise test case execution
results. By applying significant value reduction, the algorithm's runtime is
optimized for optimal results on large-scale software systems. This paper also
proposes a parallelized version of the algorithm to enhance its efficiency and
effectiveness, utilizing general-purpose Tez/HDInsight systems.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored.

Initially, the Lawrence-Doniach and interlayer tunneling models were the prominent theoretical concepts to describe cuprate superconductors by connecting CuO planes with Josephson couplings. Yet, the discovery of fragmented Fermi surfaces at CuO plane edges just before charge gaps was found in 2007, called "nested arcs", made these theories insufficient. In response, we are proposing an expansion of the interlayer tunneling Hamiltonian to incorporate nested arcs and add the coupling of separate plane patches and separate column sites. We call this modified theory the "patch-column nested arc charge superconducting model", and and and predict that when charges were delocalized at column sites in 2018, nested arcs should vanish, and superconducting gaps should appear all over the CuO plane Fermi surfaces.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark equation of state and the associated properties of the quark star radius.

The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping constitutes a new NP-complete problem. We also present a polynomial-time algorithm to solve this maximum-weight anti Tai mapping problem for any subset of node labels.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior, maintaining variance equivalence when measured in opposite directions. Furthermore, they display identical mean squared displacement performance. It is observed that increased initial mean displacement variance leads to decreased effective squeezing variance, whereas increased initial variance in number states varies differently. Variance equivalence can be attained when the mean displacement variance exceeds effective squeezing variance by a factor of at least three. Variational analysis reveals that states with similar variance in both quadratures as the compass state minimize uncertainty, thereby optimizing estimation accuracy. Ultimately, these findings suggest that states resembling the compass state in the Fock space possess the capacity for precise estimation of small displacements.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they remain unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. In these flawed approaches, triggers that are activated after each layer's output is pooled through a global averaging method are subject to alteration during the training process, causing them to become unpredictable and unreliable. Given that the defense against poisons that embed these kinds of triggers is non-existent without compromising performance, we investigate a novel approach of employing triggers that are both location and pattern dependent, presenting challenges that are comparable to encountering fortified castle defenses. We also present summaries of several attempts at implementing these kinds of triggers, along with the obstacles they present, including a case study of a trigger framework called DBL that applies these kinds of triggers after the final layer of a network with global average pooling, along with its associated challenges.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor analyzed is the PPN parameter gamma, which has a significant impact on light propagation and can lead to discrepancies if set to an incorrect value. Researchers have estimated a global impact of small deviations in gamma on parallax measurements made by missions like Gaia, contributing to the uncertainty in determining the Hubble constant. Given its unlikely magnitude, the influence of a flawed PPN gamma parameter on light distortion is minimal in comparison to the noise generated by various other influences, including a global shift in parallax that contributes to its uncertainty. This contribution can be expressed in microarcseconds as approximately 2 times the standard deviation of the parallax distribution minus the mean parallax, divided by the standard deviation of the diagonal elements of the noise matrix representing a global parallax distortion due to a faulty PPN gamma value.

We have developed an efficient approach for condensing complex systems into their fundamental behaviors using their primary underlying features. By leveraging observed data, we pinpoint a low-dimensional structure that characterizes the systems' gradual evolution and generate an extremely simple representation of the systems' dynamics within that structure. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies implicit optimization to fit a system's underlying structure to available data and simplifies the systems' dynamics, we have created two more direct methods that transform the process into explicit problems under specific assumptions. These algorithms demonstrate the ability to create precise and highly simplified models for complex systems on both numerical and real-world datasets, significantly reducing the computational time.

Certain fundamental models which result in one- and two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems, such as the Schrödinger equation, but the search continues in non-linear contexts. This report is to self-accelerating solitons description within the framework of the two-component Gross-Pitaevskii equations.

This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client, who is determined to tamper with input data and has access to all system parameters including the secure multi-party computation (MPC) protocol being used. Although multiple studies have developed MPC-based protocols for secure inference, there is room for enhancement in their efficiency. We introduce a novel approach, an improved MPC-based secure inference method, that significantly reduces communication overhead by leveraging organized data access patterns within an MySQL database, allowing for a more than ten-fold reduction in communication costs compared to existing solutions.

Our research on the M101 galaxy group and its surrounding area used data from the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope, specifically looking for effects of the M101 galaxy's gravity on nearby neutral hydrogen gas.  90 percent of space around galaxies is composed of neutral hydrogen gas, which is a critical component for understanding how stars are formed.   Although M101 has a rich supply of neutral hydrogen gas within its disk, observations show that there is an additional gas present outside its disk.   By analyzing temperature, velocity, and density maps of hydrogen gas, we have found a region of extra-gas hovering above the northern edge of the galaxy's disk.   Although further research is necessary to confirm this finding with greater certainty, we believe this external gas may be influenced by the galaxy's gravity alone.   Although a region of high-velocity gas was found in the southern edge of the galaxy's disk, there was not a distinct region of low-density gas found above it.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary gases. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and clearer spectral features, current spectral analyses are constrained by a lack of comprehensive reference data. Our initial investigation identified a substantial knowledge deficit in cometary spectra for several common oxygen-based molecular cations, namely H2O+, NO+, and CO+. To address this issue, we produced simulated spectral profiles for these molecules within the 300-1000 nm range, with a focus on their photoionization solar spectrum interaction. Additionally, we compiled available experimental and astronomical data on comet and planetary atmosphere observations, as well as comet mass spectrometry data, to further enrich our analysis of molecular cation spectra.

The challenge of representing a positive entity as a sum of squared components dates back centuries to notable mathematicians Bachet and Lagrange. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other fundamental structures and fields. In this study, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global domain (either a number domain or a global function domain) into the sum of the minimal-length squared components.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances, atomic spin states, and exoplanets.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

The provided article introduces an Itô-Wentzell type formula tailored to accommodate paths with α-Hölder regularity of $\alpha$ within the interval $(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{2}]$. Additionally, it expands on prior work by R. Castrequini and P. Catuogno concerning Young integrals, as well as research by C. Keller and J. Zhang on rough paths.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues. A novel approach is proposed that leverages random walk models to tackle these issues. This approach involves each node simulating a random walk on the graph, sharing the collected samples with the server, and training a unified model on the collected data. Experimental results show that our proposed approach outperforms existing algorithms such as FedAvg and KWoOLM in terms of accuracy and efficiency, particularly when dealing with low communication scenarios.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize more sensitive and high-speed FPGA systems, thereby significantly reducing initial trigger latency and increasing its sensitivity to physics events. As part of this project, a new ATLAS-FCT board has been designed and manufactured, leveraging multiple high-speed transceivers on an UltraScale+ FPGA to efficiently route calibration data among the jet calorimeter modules. The ATLAS-FCT serves as both a system controller and ultra-high speed router, effectively bridging the gap between the various calibration requirements of the JC38 electronic system and the custom serialized data format of the FCTs. Furthermore, a new real-time calibration algorithm titled ATLAS-FCT Calib has been developed to restore the energy response of hadronic jets, achieving a remarkable 2% restoration within two standard deviations.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations and potential misalignments, which can otherwise
jeopardize the rendering pipeline. To address these challenges for realistic virtual
human avatars, we developed Articulated Neural Rendering, a new framework that
integrates unmodeled deformations with DNR through loss function optimization. This
novel approach enables ANR to generate photorealistic avatars from video input, and
further testing with limited training data revealed ANR's robust performance even when
presented with unfamiliar scenes.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be harnessed to analyse 
the stability of atomic configurations, thus revealing the characteristics 
required for phase transitions and disordered states. Overall, our framework 
offers a highly adaptable and versatile solution for examining complex materials 
by uniting the strengths of machine learning and traditional materials science.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's proof format debuted,  
which has undergone significant evolution ever since. veriT's proofs have found a  
wide range of applications and numerous solvers now generate proofs in this same  
format. As the next step in further improvement, we would appreciate input from  
other solvers in order to incorporate best practices and best practices ever more  
effectively.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER).

Graph mining applications rely heavily on node embeddings that preserve structure and proximity. To test the validity of novel node embedding techniques, a limited range of benchmark datasets is typically used. In this study, a new diverse social network dataset, Twitch Gamers, has been created to provide a range of target attributes. The evaluation of the social network and the results of the node classification experiments confirm that Twitch Gamers can effectively assess the performance of novel node embedding algorithms.

Our study proposes that a previous observation made by Belle and BaBar of a complex spin state at around $1500$, which had been interpreted as a single entity or combination of multiple spin states, is now identified as the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance reported by LHCb in recent times.  Employing a perturbative QCD approach, we calculate the di-kaon distribution amplitudes from LHCb data, specifically from quasi-two-body $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$ decays containing the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance.  The calculated distributions can be used to explain BaBar's measurements of the $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$ decay at an invariant mass $M(K^+K^-)\sim 1.5$ GeV, showing the contribution from $\rho^0(1450)$. Moreover, the observed structure around $1.5$ GeV in $B^+ \to K^+K_S K_S$ spectrum may correspond to $\rho^0(1450)$ as well.  The theoretical estimates of branching fractions and for $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$, also include the direct $S$-wave contributions.  Furthermore, we show that the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance can be

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams. Furthermore, we've identified problems with primordial black holes that are dark matter when considering that they might acquire a charge through swamping and that this could lead to the accretion of ordinary matter.

A novel algorithm for precise force control in series elastic actuators is introduced in this paper, centered on a cutting-edge force estimation technique called the transmission force observer. This approach was developed to enhance the inaccurate force readings caused by the nonlinear elastic transmission and sensor measurement errors of the actuators' deformation sensors. The study first critiques conventional SEA force sensing methods, examining their stochastic properties that ultimately enable accurate force control through the proposed transmission force observer. A critical parameter derived from system analysis is key in optimizing the performance of the force-controlled system, guiding the achievement of the optimal outcome.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account provides a useful framework for predicting the breakdown of membranes, skins, and other similar structures.

We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate, multi-component complex scalar fields. These scalar fields are part of the fundamental representation of both the SU(Nc) gauge group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group. We've investigated their interactions within a general quartic potential that is compatible with the global and gauge symmetries. By analyzing minimum-energy configurations and performing Monte Carlo simulations, we've studied the phase diagrams, Higgs phases, and corresponding symmetry-breaking patterns. The influence of the quartic potential has also been considered. Additionally, we explored whether lattice model transitions relate to the behavior of continuum field theory at its stable charged fixed points, particularly for Nc=Nf=2, showing signs of an SU(Nc) Higgs phase under specific conditions.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we established precise update rules for the mean and covariance.  By applying the rules to the covariance, we derived a connection between our method and Brownian motion.  By testing our approach on a remotely operated vehicle, we demonstrated its effectiveness in reaching targets, utilizing fewer data samples for SPGA to plan optimal paths.

This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds for sorting networks with specific pre-determined constant depths. Moreover, we developed sorting algorithms that correspond to our lower bounds for constants k and d when n is sufficiently large, based on Bennett's construction, we derived a sorting network with a minimum number of comparators (k) for each constant depth (d).

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts.

Using recent observations, we create a set of models for a galaxy like the Milky Way. By combining collisionless and gaseous particle simulations, we observe that a bar forms in the center within one billion years, along with spiral arms composed of 2, 3, and 4-armed patterns. These features persist for at least 3 billion years in our simulations. However, we find that a bar won't develop if the galaxy's disk has a radial scale longer than 2.6 kiloparsecs. Additionally, we observe a resonance circle forming at 4.2 kiloparsecs in a typical galaxy model, causing a pattern speed of 40.8 km/s/kpc. This feature is significant as it may affect the formation of planets in solar systems.

Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxy combinations that significantly alter galaxy morphology. This study focuses on how magnetic fields affect major mergers involving abundant gas, using high-resolution simulations to examine the impact. Conducting this analysis within a realistic cosmic framework, this study employs advanced simulations to compare magnetic field effects on merging galaxies with and without magnetic field influence. Unlike previous non-realistic simulations, this study discovers that incorporating magnetic fields in simulations of massive galaxy mergers has a notable impact on how these galaxy combinations solidify. Although magnetic fields do not greatly alter general features, they have a notable effect on structural characteristics, forming extended discs and spiral patterns in simulations, whereas simulations without magnetic fields yield more compact, ring-like structures. A separate investigation on resolution demonstrates that global features converge across various levels of resolution and physical modeling but reveals distinct differences in galaxy morphology at sufficient resolution, attributed to enhanced amplification of magnetic fields in high-resolution simulations, effectively impacting gas dynamics.

Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. These lesion masks were used in conjunction with the original CT scans to generate additional useful information. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss into our improved Contrastive Mixup Classification network. Consequently, our approach earned top honors with a Macro F1 Score of 51.76%, outperforming the baseline by a substantial 11.46%.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences.

Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have not been extensively explored. To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using rounded averages, specifically when U equals the average of Y divided by n. Theoretical measures including the probability generating function, expected value, and variance are utilized to analyze how rounding impacts data and assess the impact on distribution parameter estimators. Our analysis reveals that in certain cases, rounding has a minimal effect but can severely distort results in other situations as demonstrated through practical applications. The simple techniques proposed are capable of mitigating the impact of rounding errors to some extent.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal material, GdInO3, employing X-ray and neutron diffraction methods, as well as direct current susceptibility and Gd203 differential neutron spectroscopy. Two structural phases were identified in Gd203, characterized by centered honeycomb lattices and overlapping triangular grids. The center of the honeycomb unit cell contains a single atom, while there are three atoms per unit cell in the Gd203 phase. The materials share the same space group, R-3, but differ in their transition temperatures from 925 K to 825 K. The ground state of the Gd203 phase exhibits net magnetization aligned with the three-fold axis, while the Gd203 phase displays in-plane ordered moments. The transition of the Gd203 phase was found to be of a second-order, while the Gd203 phase exhibited both first and second-order aspects in its transition.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions are additive, is examined in a setting that considers both Nash equilibria and fairness principles. Our analysis covers two scenarios: when the goods are valued independently and when they are interdependently valued. For independent valuations, we establish bounds for multiplicative approximate fairness in Nash equilibria, while for interdependent valuations, we investigate the existence of Pareto optimal and equitable Nash equilibria.
